strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: inaccurate imputation of sensitive attributes can undermine fairness interventions. Training the imputer adversarially offers a plausible extension of FairGNN.

The reported improvements are promising. On BAIL, BFtS improves AVPR/F1 from FairGNN’s 0.83/0.86 to 0.88/0.91 while reducing the equality-of-opportunity gap from 4.1% to 1.7%. German also shows substantial fairness improvements with comparable F1.

The evaluation includes four real datasets, synthetic graphs with varying assortativity, GCN and GAT architectures, ten runs, and accuracy–fairness trade-off plots. The appendix provides sensitivity analyses, LDAM ablations, pseudocode, and a code link.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees do not establish the claimed behavior of the actual training objective. Equation 7 drops the classification and imputation losses from Equations 4 and 6, while Proposition 1 replaces the parameterized, regularized imputer with an unspecified supremum over imputations. Minimizing classification loss plus a finite fairness penalty need not achieve zero divergence, so Theorem 1 does not establish demographic parity for the trained model. The admissible imputation set and assumptions connecting the analysis to training need explicit treatment.

The convergence argument contains mathematical errors. Section 5.3 states that distributions with disjoint supports have Jensen–Shannon divergence zero; their divergence is maximal, equal to log 2 under natural logarithms. Constant imputations also leave one conditioning group empty rather than defining two distributions with disjoint supports. Moreover, the inequality in Corollary 1 does not establish improved gradients or convergence. These problems undermine a stated theoretical contribution.

Figure 3(a) plots an RNF result near 1−ΔDP = −2, although Equation 9 requires both ΔDP and 1−ΔDP to lie in [0,1]. This requires correction or an explanation of any failure-value convention before the synthetic comparison can be trusted. Table 1’s caption also overstates NBA performance: BFtS has lower AVPR and F1 than Vanilla.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution. BFtS changes both the imputation objective and the classification/imputation losses. Table 3 varies where LDAM is applied but provides no otherwise identical β=0 comparison or FairGNN baseline using the same LDAM losses. The paper itself attributes BAIL’s accuracy gains to LDAM, making these controls particularly important.

The missingness evaluation does not sufficiently test the motivating concern about biased data collection. The manuscript varies the observed fraction from 20% to 50% of training nodes but does not clearly specify the sampling mechanism or evaluate missingness dependent on sensitive group, outcome, or features. It also lacks quantitative evidence showing how closely the learned imputations approach worst-case bias or how much conventional imputations underestimate true bias.

The method description leaves consequential implementation ambiguities. Equation 2 uses classifier outputs in the imputation-loss denominator, and Figure 2’s caption reverses the classifier/adversary optimization directions relative to Equations 4–5. The paper also does not explain how gradients pass through the imputed group assignments in Equation 3. These details are essential for reproducing the proposed adversarial imputer.
